name: Acetaldehyde
description: Sharp, green-apple, raw pumpkin, or fresh latex paint note indicating incomplete fermentation or premature packaging.
aromaPerception: Green apple skin, freshly cut pumpkin, wet emulsion paint, or bruised apple.
flavorPerception: Tart, raw green apple with a cidery, unripe finish.
mouthfeelPerception: No direct mouthfeel impact; can accentuate perceived thinness.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Ethyl Hexanoate (Red Apple Ester): Acetaldehyde smells sharp, raw, and paint-like (unripe green apple), whereas ethyl hexanoate is sweet, ripe, and fruity.
vs. Grassy (Hexanal): Acetaldehyde has a pungent apple/latex edge, whereas hexanal smells like crushed green leaves or lawn clippings.
vs. Cider Acidity: In ciders, crisp malic tartness is clean fruit acid; acetaldehyde tastes flat, green, and paint-like.
typicalOrigins: Beer racked off yeast or cold-crashed too early before yeast finished reducing acetaldehyde to ethanol.
Under-pitching, low dissolved oxygen, or stressed/unhealthy yeast.
Post-packaging oxidation converting ethanol back into acetaldehyde.
Bacterial spoilage (Acetobacter or Zymomonas) in finished beer.
preventionTips: Pitch an adequate, healthy yeast cell count and aerate wort properly prior to pitching.
Allow a warm conditioning rest at the end of primary fermentation before crashing or packaging.
Minimize oxygen pickup during transfer, bottling, and kegging.
whenAppropriate: Almost always a fault in beer, mead, and cider. Trace levels may appear in very young Budweiser-style American Lagers, but noticeable green-apple or paint notes are penalized.

name: Alcoholic / Fusel
description: Hot, spicy, peppery alcohol heat that burns the throat and nostrils, distinct from smooth ethanol warmth.
aromaPerception: Sharp, pungent alcohol vapors, spicy spirits, or mild sherry-like heat.
flavorPerception: Harsh, biting, peppery spirit flavor that overwhelms delicate malt or honey.
mouthfeelPerception: Prickly, burning warming sensation down the throat and on the palate.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Clean Ethanol Warmth: Normal high-ABV warmth feels smooth and comforting in the chest; fusel alcohols sting the nostrils and burn sharply at the back of the throat.
vs. Solvent (Ethyl Acetate): Fusels give a hot, spicy spirit burn, whereas solvent smells specifically like acetone or nail polish remover.
vs. Hop/Phenolic Spice: Fusel heat is an alcoholic sting rather than herbal, woody, or clove-like spice.
typicalOrigins: Fermenting too warm, especially during the first 48 hours of active growth.
Under-pitching or nutrient-deficient must/wort (especially in mead without staggered nutrients).
Excessive simple sugars or prolonged contact with dead yeast trub.
preventionTips: Control fermentation temperature tightly within the yeast strain's lower-to-mid range during active growth.
Pitch healthy yeast at proper rates and provide adequate yeast nutrition (YAN in mead/cider).
Use balanced wort oxygenation without over-aerating.
whenAppropriate: Smooth warming alcohol is expected in Barleywines, Eisbock, Wee Heavy, and Sack Meads, but harsh or burning fusels are always a fault.

name: Autolysis
typicalConcentration: Negligible in fresh beer; rises with prolonged yeast contact
description: Savory, meaty, soy sauce, Vegemite, or burnt-rubber character caused by decaying yeast cells.
aromaPerception: Beef bouillon, soy sauce, Marmite/Vegemite, burnt rubber, or sulfury meat broth.
flavorPerception: Savory umami, salty meat extract, stale yeast, and rubbery bitterness.
mouthfeelPerception: Heavy, brothy, sometimes slightly oily finish.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Dark Malt Roast/Melanoidin: Dark malts provide clean coffee, cocoa, or toasted bread; autolysis tastes distinctly savory like beef broth, soy sauce, or burnt rubber.
vs. Yeasty: Fresh yeast tastes bready and doughy; autolysis tastes decayed, meaty, and sulfurous.
vs. Mercaptan: Mercaptan is sharper rotten cabbage/drain gas; autolysis is savory broth and rubber.
typicalOrigins: Leaving beer sitting on a thick primary yeast cake for months at warm temperatures.
Pitching old, low-viability yeast or fermenting under high hydrostatic pressure.
Warm storage of unfiltered bottle-conditioned beer.
preventionTips: Rack beer off primary yeast trub once fermentation and conditioning are complete.
Pitch fresh, high-viability yeast and store finished beer cold.
Avoid prolonged warm aging on heavy lees unless intentionally making sur lie styles.
whenAppropriate: Almost always a fault in beer. Very subtle savory/brioche autolytic complexity can be acceptable in aged Champagne-method ciders or Traditional Perry.

name: Caprylic / Goaty
description: Waxy, tallow, goaty, or soapy-fatty character from medium-chain fatty acids released by stressed or aging yeast.
aromaPerception: Wet goat hair, candle wax, tallow, or faint rancid soap.
flavorPerception: Waxy, soapy, fatty bitterness with a slightly cheesy/goaty edge.
mouthfeelPerception: Waxy, greasy coating on the tongue and roof of the mouth.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Isovaleric (Cheesy): Isovaleric smells like sweaty socks or aged parmesan from old hops; caprylic is waxy, tallow-like, and soapy.
vs. Alkaline (Soapy): Alkaline feels chalky and flat from high pH or cleaner residue; caprylic feels waxy/greasy from fatty acids.
vs. Brettanomyces Funk: Clean Brett adds barnyard leather or horse blanket without waxy tallow.
typicalOrigins: Yeast stress, poor wort aeration, or prolonged aging on yeast sediment.
Weak or stuck fermentations releasing medium-chain fatty acids.
Contamination by certain wild yeasts or aged bottle conditioning.
preventionTips: Ensure healthy yeast viability, proper aeration, and timely racking off trub.
Maintain steady fermentation temperatures and avoid nutrient starvation.
whenAppropriate: Subtle caprylic notes can appear in aged Lambic, Gueuze, or Old Ale, but prominent goaty or waxy character is a fault in clean styles.

name: Diacetyl
description: Rich butter, butterscotch, or artificial movie-popcorn aroma and flavor paired with a slick, oily palate.
aromaPerception: Melted butter, butterscotch candy, movie theater popcorn, or toffee.
flavorPerception: Sweetish artificial butter or butterscotch that lingers on the finish.
mouthfeelPerception: Slick, oily, tongue-coating sensation.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Caramel/Crystal Malt: Caramel malts taste like toasted sugar or clean toffee with no oily mouthfeel; diacetyl smells like warm movie-popcorn butter and leaves a slick coating on the tongue.
vs. Butyric Acid: Diacetyl is sweet/pleasant butterscotch; butyric is putrid, rancid butter or baby vomit.
vs. Oxidation (Sherry/Toffee): Oxidation brings papery staleness; diacetyl is distinctly buttery and slick.
typicalOrigins: Natural fermentation intermediate (from alpha-acetolactate) not reabsorbed by yeast.
Chilling or racking beer off the yeast before a diacetyl rest is complete.
Early-flocculating yeast strains dropping out too soon, or oxygen pickup post-fermentation.
Lactic acid bacteria contamination (especially Pediococcus) in packaged beer or dirty draft lines.
preventionTips: Perform a 2–3 day diacetyl rest (raising temp 3–5°F / 2–3°C) near the end of primary fermentation.
Pitch healthy yeast, ensure adequate aeration, and verify clean draft lines and cold-side sanitation.
whenAppropriate: Low levels are traditional and permissible in Czech Pale/Premium Pale Lagers and British Bitters/Scottish Ales. A fault in clean German lagers, American ales, mead, and cider.

name: Estery
chemicalCompound: Isoamyl Acetate, Ethyl Hexanoate, Ethyl Acetate
description: Pronounced fruity aromas and flavors—banana, pear drop, red apple, or bubblegum—out of place in clean styles.
aromaPerception: Banana, Juicy Fruit gum, pear drop, red apple, strawberry, or tropical fruit.
flavorPerception: Sweet, fruity ester character that can mask malt or hop balance.
mouthfeelPerception: No direct mouthfeel impact; can increase perceived sweetness.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Hop Fruitiness: Hop citrus/tropical notes come with resinous/pine/floral hop oils and bitterness; fermentation esters smell like banana, pear, or bubblegum.
vs. Acetaldehyde: Ripe red-apple ester (ethyl hexanoate) is sweet and fruity, whereas acetaldehyde is raw, green, and paint-like.
vs. Solvent: Low ethyl acetate is pear-like; high concentrations cross into nail polish remover.
typicalOrigins: Fermenting above the yeast strain's optimal temperature range.
Under-pitching yeast or low wort oxygenation (forcing longer yeast growth).
High-gravity wort concentrating ester synthesis, or choosing an expressive ale strain for a clean style.
preventionTips: Ferment within the strain's recommended temperature range, especially during the first 72 hours.
Pitch an appropriate cell count and oxygenate wort adequately.
whenAppropriate: Essential in Weissbier, Belgian Ales, Saison, English Bitters, and many ciders/meads. Considered a fault in German Pils, Munich Helles, and clean American lagers.

name: Solvent
description: Harsh, chemical nail-polish remover, acetone, or model-glue aroma and flavor.
aromaPerception: Acetone, nail polish remover, paint thinner, lacquer, or model airplane glue.
flavorPerception: Sharp, chemical, artificial fruit-solvent bite that dominates the palate.
mouthfeelPerception: Hot, astringent, chemical warming sensation.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Estery (Pear Drop): Ethyl acetate smells pleasantly pear-like at low ppm, but becomes unmistakably acetone/nail-polish remover above threshold.
vs. Alcoholic / Fusel: Fusels are spicy/hot spirit warmth; solvent has a volatile chemical lacquer/acetone aroma.
vs. Acetic: Acetic is sharp vinegar sourness; solvent is volatile chemical nail-polish remover (though Acetobacter + ethanol can form ethyl acetate).
typicalOrigins: Excessively warm primary fermentation temperatures.
Severe yeast stress, under-pitching, or high-gravity osmotic shock.
Aerobic bacterial or wild yeast contamination (e.g., Acetobacter or Hansenula) producing ethyl acetate.
preventionTips: Keep active fermentation temperatures tightly controlled and cool during peak krausen.
Pitch healthy yeast with proper nutrients and oxygen, and prevent aerobic microbial contamination.
whenAppropriate: Always a fault in clean beer, mead, and cider. Trace ethyl acetate complexity is tolerated only in very small amounts in Flanders Red or Lambic.

name: Sulfur (H₂S)
description: Rotten eggs (H₂S) or struck-match / burning sulfur (SO₂) character from active or stressed yeast metabolism.
aromaPerception: Rotten eggs, sewer gas (H₂S), or struck matchstick / mineral spring water (SO₂).
flavorPerception: Sulfurous, eggy, or sharp matchstick mineral tang.
mouthfeelPerception: SO₂ can cause a slight prickly throat irritation at high levels.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Mercaptan: H₂S smells like fresh rotten eggs and often vents off with CO₂; mercaptan smells like rotten cabbage, garlic, or drain gas and does not age out.
vs. DMS: DMS is sweet cooked corn/tomato; sulfur is eggy or matchstick-like.
vs. Burton Snatch (Mineral Water): Subtle sulfury crispness in Burton pale ales or lagers is clean mineral/matchstick, not putrid rotten egg.
typicalOrigins: Normal byproduct of lager, cider, and mead yeast metabolism that hasn't finished venting.
Nitrogen/YAN deficiency (very common in mead and cider) causing yeast to strip sulfur from amino acids.
Stressed yeast, poor aeration, or bacterial contamination.
preventionTips: Allow adequate conditioning/lagering time for volatile H₂S to off-gas naturally.
Provide proper yeast nutrients (especially staggered YAN in mead and cider) and healthy pitching rates.
Ensure a vigorous boil to drive off volatile sulfur precursors in wort.
whenAppropriate: Low, crisp matchstick sulfur is permissible in fresh German/Czech lagers, Burton-style English ales, and young ciders. Prominent rotten-egg H₂S is always a fault.

name: Yeasty
description: Fresh bread dough, baker's yeast, or chalky yeast-bite character from excessive yeast in suspension.
aromaPerception: Active baker's yeast, raw bread dough, or yeasty slurry.
flavorPerception: Doughy, bready, slightly sharp or chalky yeast taste.
mouthfeelPerception: Thick, powdery, chalky, or slightly astringent yeast bite.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Bready Malt (Munich/Vienna/Biscuit): Malts taste like baked bread crust or crackers; suspended yeast tastes like raw wet bread dough and leaves a powdery yeast bite.
vs. Autolysis: Fresh yeast is doughy and bready; autolysis is decayed, meaty, soy-sauce, or rubbery.
typicalOrigins: Packaging beer too early before yeast has flocculated out of suspension.
Low-flocculating yeast strain without sufficient cold crash or fining.
Rough pouring or agitation of bottle-conditioned sediment.
preventionTips: Cold-crash beer thoroughly before packaging or serving.
Use finings (gelatin, Biofine) or allow extended cold conditioning.
Pour bottle-conditioned beers gently, leaving the yeast cake behind (unless style dictates swirling).
whenAppropriate: Expected at light-to-moderate levels in German Weissbier, Dunkles Weissbier, and Witbier. A fault in bright lagers, clear ales, mead, and cider.

name: Alkaline
description: Chalky, baking-soda, or soapy flavor with a flat, flabby bitterness caused by high mash/sparge pH or un-rinsed cleaner.
aromaPerception: Minimal; occasional faint soapy or detergent-like note if from cleaner residue.
flavorPerception: Baking soda, chalky mineral, soapy, or dull, muddled bitterness.
mouthfeelPerception: Dry, chalky, slick-soapy coating on the palate.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Astringent (Tannins): Astringency puckers the gums like wet tea bags; alkaline tastes flat, chalky, or soapy like baking soda.
vs. Caprylic / Goaty: Caprylic is waxy and goat-like from fatty acids; alkaline is chalky and detergent-like.
typicalOrigins: Brewing water with excessive carbonate/bicarbonate residual alkalinity without acid or dark-malt buffering.
Over-addition of chalk (CaCO₃) or baking soda to the mash.
Inadequate rinsing of caustic, PBW, or alkaline draft-line cleaners.
preventionTips: Test brewing water alkalinity and adjust mash/sparge pH to 5.2 – 5.6 using lactic/phosphoric acid or acidulated malt.
Thoroughly rinse all fermenters, kegs, and draft lines after alkaline cleaning.
whenAppropriate: Always a fault.

name: Astringent
description: Harsh, drying, mouth-puckering sensation like chewing grape skins or over-steeped black tea.
aromaPerception: None (polyphenols are non-volatile).
flavorPerception: Harsh, woody, tea-like bitterness on the back of the tongue.
mouthfeelPerception: Drying, puckering, sandpapery sensation on gums and cheeks.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Hop Bitterness: Hop bitterness sits cleanly on the tongue and fades; astringency physically dries and puckers the gums and cheeks like a wet tea bag.
vs. Husky / Grainy: Husky adds raw grain/straw flavor alongside dryness; astringency is pure mouth-drying tannin.
vs. Cider/Melomel Fruit Tannins: Bittersweet cider apples and dark berry skins provide structured, pleasant tannin; grain-husk astringency feels harsh and papery.
typicalOrigins: Sparging too hot (> 170°F / 77°C) or letting sparge runoff pH rise above 6.0.
Over-sparging (collecting runoff below 1.010 SG) or over-crushing grain husks.
Excessive dry-hop polyphenol extraction or steeping dark/roasted grains too hot.
preventionTips: Keep sparge water below 170°F (77°C) and acidify sparge water to keep pH under 5.8.
Stop sparging before runoff gravity drops below 1.010, and avoid pulverizing grain husks.
whenAppropriate: Pleasant, structured tannins are essential in English/French Ciders, Traditional Perry, and dark fruit Melomels. Harsh grain-husk astringency is always a fault in beer.

name: DMS (Dimethyl Sulfide)
description: Cooked sweet corn, creamed corn, or tomato-sauce aroma and flavor from volatile sulfur compounds.
aromaPerception: Cooked sweet corn, creamed corn, canned corn, or cooked tomato juice.
flavorPerception: Sweetish cooked vegetable / creamed corn character.
mouthfeelPerception: No direct mouthfeel impact.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Flaked Corn / Maize Adjuncts: Corn adjuncts in Cream Ale or Pre-Prohibition Lager taste like clean, sweet cornmeal or dry tortilla; DMS tastes specifically like steamed/canned creamed corn.
vs. Vegetal: DMS is sweet corn/tomato; vegetal is cooked cabbage, celery, or rotting vegetables.
vs. Sulfur (H₂S): H₂S is rotten eggs; DMS is sweet cooked corn.
typicalOrigins: Weak or covered boil failing to volatilize DMS formed from S-methyl-methionine (SMM) in pale/Pilsner malts.
Slow wort chilling above 140°F (60°C), allowing SMM to keep converting to DMS after the boil ends.
Wort-spoilage bacteria (e.g., Obesumbacterium) during slow fermentation startup.
preventionTips: Maintain a vigorous, uncovered rolling boil (especially for Pilsner-malt beers, 60–90 minutes).
Chill wort rapidly below 140°F (60°C) immediately after flameout and keep cold-side sanitation tight.
whenAppropriate: Very low background levels are acceptable in Cream Ale, German Helles, and some pale lagers. Distinct cooked-corn DMS is a fault in ales and most lagers.

name: Husky / Grainy
description: Raw grain husk, straw, or harsh dry cereal character from shredded husks or poor lautering.
aromaPerception: Raw cracked barley, dry straw, chaff, or damp grain silo.
flavorPerception: Raw cereal husk, grassy graininess, and dry husk bitterness.
mouthfeelPerception: Dry, scratchy, mildly astringent finish.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Crisp Malt Graininess (Pilsner/Pale Malt): Clean Pilsner malt tastes like sweet water crackers or honeyed bread; husky tastes like raw chaff, dry straw, and scratchy husks.
vs. Astringent: Astringency is pure gum-puckering tannin; husky pairs dry mouthfeel with raw grain/straw flavor.
typicalOrigins: Over-crushing malt so husks are pulverized into fine shreds.
High sparge temperature or high sparge pH extracting husk compounds.
Very high proportion of unmalted or high-husk adjunct grains without proper mash pH.
preventionTips: Widen grain mill gap slightly to crack kernels cleanly while keeping husks intact.
Monitor mash/sparge pH (< 5.8) and keep sparge water under 170°F (77°C).
whenAppropriate: Light, crisp graininess is appropriate in German Pils, Munich Helles, and Cream Ale, but harsh husky chaff is always a fault.

name: Acetic
description: Sharp, pungent vinegar aroma and acrid sourness produced by acetic acid bacteria in the presence of oxygen.
aromaPerception: White vinegar, cider vinegar, or sharp volatile acidity that prickles the nose.
flavorPerception: Sharp, biting vinegar sourness (often paired with ethyl acetate).
mouthfeelPerception: Sharp, biting acidity on the sides of the tongue and back of the throat.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Lactic Acid: Lactic is clean, soft, yogurt-like tartness with no aroma; acetic has a sharp vinegar aroma that stings the nostrils.
vs. Citric / Malic Fruit Acid: Fruit acids taste bright and refreshing; acetic tastes unmistakably like salad vinegar.
vs. Solvent: Solvent smells like nail polish remover; acetic smells like vinegar (though both frequently co-occur).
typicalOrigins: Contamination by Acetobacter or Gluconobacter bacteria.
Oxygen exposure in fermented beer/mead/cider (e.g., loose airlocks, headspace in kegs/carboys, fruit flies).
Contaminated wood barrels or porous plastic equipment.
preventionTips: Eliminate oxygen pickup post-fermentation and keep airlocks filled and sealed.
Keep fruit flies away from fermenters and sanitize or replace scratched plastic gear.
whenAppropriate: Complex, balanced acetic character is traditional in Flanders Red Ale, Oud Bruin, and Lambic. Always a fault in clean beers, mead, and standard ciders.

name: Butyric
description: Putrid, rancid butter, baby vomit, or spoiled milk aroma caused by anaerobic bacterial spoilage.
aromaPerception: Baby vomit, rancid butter, spoiled milk, or Limburger cheese.
flavorPerception: Nauseating, cheesy, sour-rancid butter flavor.
mouthfeelPerception: Oily, unpleasant lingering coating.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Diacetyl: Diacetyl smells like sweet movie-popcorn butter or butterscotch; butyric smells putrid, sour, and unmistakably like vomit or rancid butter.
vs. Isovaleric: Isovaleric is dry sweaty socks or aged parmesan from old hops; butyric is wet, sour vomit.
typicalOrigins: Anaerobic bacteria (Clostridium) thriving in warm, unboiled wort or kettle-sour mashes.
Spent grain left sitting too long or mash temperatures dropping into the 90–120°F (32–49°C) danger zone.
Severe sanitation failure in wort chillers or fermentation vessels.
preventionTips: Do not allow unboiled wort or mashes to sit warm for extended periods; pre-acidify kettle sours to pH ≤ 4.5 and purge oxygen.
Clean and sanitize plate chillers, hoses, and valves thoroughly.
whenAppropriate: Always a severe fault.

name: Indole
description: Pungent fecal, pigpen, or mothball aroma from early wort infection by coliform or enteric bacteria.
aromaPerception: Barnyard manure, fecal, pigpen, outhouse, or mothballs.
flavorPerception: Unpleasant, dirty barnyard or chemical mothball taste.
mouthfeelPerception: No direct mouthfeel impact.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Brettanomyces Barnyard: Clean Brett smells like dry horse blanket, saddle leather, or hay; indole smells distinctly fecal, like sewage or mothballs.
vs. Mercaptan: Mercaptan smells like rotten cabbage or drain gas; indole is fecal/mothball.
typicalOrigins: Enteric/coliform bacteria (Enterobacter, Klebsiella, Citrobacter) multiplying in unpitched or slow-starting wort.
Contaminated water, dirty hoses, or long lag times before yeast fermentation lowers wort pH.
preventionTips: Pitch healthy yeast promptly after chilling wort so pH drops rapidly below 4.5.
Sanitize all cold-side transfer lines, chillers, and fermenters rigorously.
whenAppropriate: Always a fault.

name: Lactic
description: Clean, yogurt-like, or sour-milk tartness caused by lactic acid bacteria.
aromaPerception: Minimal; very faint plain yogurt or clean dairy tartness.
flavorPerception: Crisp, clean, yogurt-like or lemony sourness without vinegar bite.
mouthfeelPerception: Mouth-watering tartness and crisp, drying finish.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Acetic (Vinegar): Lactic is soft, clean, yogurt-like tartness with almost no nose; acetic has a sharp vinegar aroma.
vs. Dark Malt Acidity: Roasted malts give a dry, espresso-like tang; lactic is distinctly sour-milk/yogurt tart.
vs. Cider Malic Acid: Natural apple malic acid is bright and fruity; lactic (after malolactic conversion) tastes softer, rounder, and creamy.
typicalOrigins: Contamination by Lactobacillus or Pediococcus in hoses, valves, heat exchangers, or draft lines.
Cross-contamination from sour-beer equipment to clean-beer lines.
preventionTips: Dedicate separate plastic hoses, gaskets, and bottling wands for sour vs. clean beers.
Deep-clean and sanitize draft lines, kegs, and plate chillers regularly.
whenAppropriate: Defining characteristic in Berliner Weisse, Gose, Flanders Red, Lambic, and Traditional Farmhouse Ciders. A fault in clean lagers, ales, and standard meads.

name: Mercaptan
description: Pungent rotten cabbage, sewer drain gas, garlic, or burned-rubber sulfur aroma that will not age out.
aromaPerception: Rotten cabbage, stagnant drain gas, crushed garlic, onion, or natural gas odorant.
flavorPerception: Foul, sulfurous onion/garlic and rotting vegetable taste.
mouthfeelPerception: No direct mouthfeel impact.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Sulfur (H₂S): H₂S smells like rotten eggs and often dissipates with conditioning; mercaptan smells like garlic, onion, or sewer gas and is permanent.
vs. Vegetal: Vegetal is mild cooked cabbage/celery; mercaptan is pungent, chemical drain gas.
vs. Autolysis: Autolysis is savory meat broth/Vegemite; mercaptan is sharp sewer/garlic.
typicalOrigins: Severe yeast autolysis converting H₂S and ethanol into persistent ethanethiol.
Bacterial contamination (Zymomonas or wort-spoilage bacteria).
Light exposure or stagnant lees in un-racked mead and cider.
preventionTips: Rack finished beer, mead, and cider off dead yeast/lees promptly.
Maintain strict cold-side sanitation and protect packaged beverages from UV light.
whenAppropriate: Always a fault.

name: Phenolic
description: Spicy clove, black pepper, smoke, or wild-yeast barnyard notes produced by POF+ yeast or wild strains.
aromaPerception: Clove, nutmeg, black pepper, wood smoke, or subtle leather/barnyard.
flavorPerception: Warming baking-spice clove, peppery phenolic bite, or smoky finish.
mouthfeelPerception: Slight drying or numbing spice sensation on the tongue.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Chlorophenol (Band-Aid): Clean yeast phenols (4-VG) smell like natural clove, pepper, or smoke; chlorophenols smell sharply medicinal like Band-Aids, mouthwash, or burnt plastic.
vs. Spice Additions: Added whole cloves or peppercorns taste sharp and botanical; yeast-derived 4-VG blends smoothly with fruity esters.
typicalOrigins: Fermenting with POF+ yeast strains (Weissbier, Belgian, Saison) or Brettanomyces.
Wild yeast contamination (especially STA1+ diastaticus) in clean-beer fermenters.
Over-sparging or high mash pH releasing ferulic acid precursors.
preventionTips: If unintended, audit cold-side sanitation to eliminate wild yeast or POF+ cross-contamination.
Use POF- yeast strains for clean American, German lager, and British styles.
whenAppropriate: Signature trait in Weissbier, Dunkles Weissbier, Saison, Belgian Ales, and traditional French/English ciders. A fault in clean lagers and standard American ales.

name: Sour / Acidic
description: Unintended sharp tartness or pH drop from wild bacterial or yeast infection.
aromaPerception: Often minimal; may carry faint lemon, yogurt, or vinegar cues depending on the microbe.
flavorPerception: Sharp, tangy, lemon-like or sour acidity that thins out malt sweetness.
mouthfeelPerception: Salivating, crisp, puckering acidity along the sides of the tongue.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Crisp Carbonation Bite: High carbonation gives carbonic prickle without lasting sourness; microbial acidity lingers and makes the sides of the tongue water.
vs. Lactic vs. Acetic: Lactic is soft yogurt tartness; acetic is sharp vinegar nose; generic sour/acidic is mixed uninvited tartness.
typicalOrigins: Mixed bacterial contamination (Lactobacillus, Pediococcus, Acetobacter) in cold-side gear.
Dirty draft lines, un-sanitized keg posts, or contaminated fruit additions.
preventionTips: Disassemble and sanitize ball-valve fittings, keg poppets, and draft lines regularly.
Pasteurize or sulfite fruit additions if clean fermentation is desired.
whenAppropriate: Expected in sour beer styles, fruit meads (Melomel), and crisp ciders. Always a fault when unintended in clean beer styles.

name: THP (Mousiness)
description: Delayed Cheerios cereal, tortilla chip, or mouse-cage aftertaste triggered as saliva raises pH on the palate.
aromaPerception: Virtually undetectable in cold beer aroma (non-volatile at low pH).
flavorPerception: Delayed aftertaste (5–15 seconds after swallowing) of Cheerios, stale corn tortillas, or mouse cage.
mouthfeelPerception: Dry, stale, grain-cracker coating at the back of the palate.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Bready/Toasty Malt: Malt flavor hits immediately on the palate and smells bready in the glass; THP has zero aroma in the glass and blooms 5–15 seconds after swallowing as saliva neutralizes beer pH.
vs. DMS: DMS smells like cooked corn right in the aroma; THP is a delayed cereal/mouse-cage retronasal aftertaste.
typicalOrigins: Brettanomyces or heterofermentative Lactobacillus reacting with lysine and ethanol in the presence of oxygen.
Common in mixed-fermentation beer, natural cider, and low-SO₂ mead exposed to trace oxygen.
preventionTips: Minimize oxygen ingress during aging and packaging of mixed-fermentation beverages.
Allow sufficient bottle/keg conditioning time (Brett can sometimes reabsorb THP over months) and maintain strict sanitation.
whenAppropriate: Always a fault (even in Lambic, Saison, and natural cider, though it can fade with extended aging).

name: Catty
description: Pungent tomcat urine, blackcurrant leaf, or crushed boxwood aroma from specific hop thiols or oxidation.
aromaPerception: Tomcat spray, blackcurrant (cassis) leaves, boxwood hedge, or damp cat litter.
flavorPerception: Sharp, musky blackcurrant-leaf or catty bitterness.
mouthfeelPerception: No direct mouthfeel impact.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Lightstruck (Skunky): Lightstruck smells like skunk spray from UV light; catty smells specifically like blackcurrant leaves or tomcat urine.
vs. Dank/Resinous Hops: Modern hops (Simcoe, Citra, Galaxy) can show mild blackcurrant/cassis notes; when it crosses into ammonia-like tomcat spray, it is a fault.
typicalOrigins: Heavy use of high-thiol New World/American hops (Simcoe, Citra, Summit, Nelson Sauvin).
Oxidative aging of hop-derived compounds in packaged IPA.
preventionTips: Store hops cold and oxygen-free; blend high-thiol hops carefully.
Purge packaging of oxygen and store hop-forward beers cold.
whenAppropriate: Very subtle blackcurrant/cassis character is accepted in modern American/New World IPAs; overt tomcat urine is always a fault.

name: Grassy
description: Freshly mowed lawn, crushed green leaves, or raw chlorophyll character from heavy dry-hopping or stale malt.
aromaPerception: Fresh-cut grass, crushed green leaves, hay, or raw alfalfa.
flavorPerception: Green, herbal, chlorophyll-like bitterness.
mouthfeelPerception: Can feel slightly rough or green on the finish.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Noble Hop Herbal/Floral: Noble hops are spicy, floral, and tea-like; grassy smells specifically like wet lawn clippings or crushed leaves.
vs. Acetaldehyde: Acetaldehyde has a sharp green-apple/paint edge; grassy is purely lawn/leaf chlorophyll.
typicalOrigins: Prolonged warm dry-hopping (> 7–10 days) or high-dose pellet hops.
Poorly kilned or damp/aged malt generating hexanal.
preventionTips: Keep dry-hop contact times short (2–4 days) and store malt and hops dry, cold, and sealed.
whenAppropriate: Light freshly-cut-grass notes can be acceptable in intensely dry-hopped pale ales and IPAs, but harsh chlorophyll is a fault.

name: Isovaleric
description: Aged parmesan cheese, sweaty gym socks, or rancid foot odor caused by oxidized hop alpha acids.
aromaPerception: Stale parmesan cheese, sweaty socks, gym locker room, or old hops.
flavorPerception: Sharp, cheesy, sour-foot bitterness.
mouthfeelPerception: No direct mouthfeel impact.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Butyric: Butyric smells wet and putrid like baby vomit; isovaleric smells dry and sharp like aged parmesan or sweaty socks.
vs. Caprylic / Goaty: Caprylic is waxy tallow; isovaleric is dry aged cheese.
typicalOrigins: Using old, warm-stored, or oxidized hops (breakdown of humulone alpha acids).
Certain wild yeast or bacterial contaminations.
preventionTips: Store hops vacuum-sealed in oxygen-barrier bags in the freezer.
Smell hops before brewing—discard any that smell cheesy.
whenAppropriate: Intentional aged-hop character in Lambic/Gueuze (using debitttered aged hops), though excessive sweaty-sock cheese is a fault everywhere else.

name: Oxidized / Cardboard
description: Wet cardboard, damp paper, or stale bread character caused by oxygen pickup and warm storage.
aromaPerception: Wet corrugated cardboard, damp newsprint, or stale/musty paper.
flavorPerception: Papery, dull, lifeless malt/fruit flavor with muted hop brightness.
mouthfeelPerception: Thin, papery, slightly stale finish.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Sherry / Vinous Oxidation: Pale beers oxidize into wet cardboard (trans-2-nonenal); dark or high-ABV beers oxidize into sweet sherry, port, or almond.
vs. Musty / Corked: Musty smells like a damp basement or moldy cork; oxidized smells like clean wet cardboard.
typicalOrigins: Oxygen ingress during racking, bottling, or kegging.
Warm storage accelerating staling reactions in packaged beer.
Hot-side splashing during mashing/lautering (minor contributor compared to cold-side O₂).
preventionTips: Purge kegs, transfer lines, and bottles with CO₂ before filling.
Avoid splashing during cold-side transfers and store finished beer cold.
whenAppropriate: Always a fault.

name: Sherry / Vinous
description: Sweet Oloroso sherry, port wine, raisin, or marzipan-almond oxidation character in aged dark or strong beverages.
aromaPerception: Oloroso sherry, port wine, dried fig, raisin, or sweet almond.
flavorPerception: Rich, wine-like oxidized sweetness with dried-fruit and nutty notes.
mouthfeelPerception: Smooth, slightly warming, wine-like finish.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Dark Crystal Malt (Special B / Plum): Dark crystal malts taste like fresh caramel, plum, and fig without wine-like alcohol oxidation; sherry oxidation adds a distinct fortified-wine/almond edge.
vs. Oxidized / Cardboard: Cardboard is papery and dull in pale beers; sherry is sweet, vinous, and nutty in dark/high-ABV beers.
typicalOrigins: Controlled or uncontrolled slow oxidation in high-gravity or dark-malt beers over months/years.
Warm cellaring or permeable bottle closures.
preventionTips: Purge headspace with CO₂ during packaging and cellar strong beers cool.
Use oxygen-absorbing caps or waxed corks for long-term aging.
whenAppropriate: Pleasant, subtle sherry complexity is prized in aged English Barleywine, Old Ale, Wee Heavy, Eisbock, and Sack Meads. A fault in fresh or pale styles.

name: Vegetal
description: Cooked cabbage, boiled celery, wet turnip, or compost aroma from aged hops, bacterial activity, or autolysis.
aromaPerception: Boiled cabbage, cooked broccoli, celery, wet turnip, or stale vegetable soup.
flavorPerception: Savory, sulfurous cooked-vegetable flavor.
mouthfeelPerception: No direct mouthfeel impact.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. DMS: DMS is specifically sweet creamed corn or tomato sauce; vegetal is boiled cabbage, celery, or turnip.
vs. Grassy: Grassy is fresh-cut raw green lawn; vegetal is cooked or decaying vegetables.
vs. Mercaptan: Mercaptan is sharp drain gas/garlic; vegetal is milder boiled cabbage.
typicalOrigins: Old or oxidized hops, or stale/damp adjuncts.
Early yeast autolysis or bacterial spoilage in wort/beer.
Excessive hop trub carried into warm fermentation.
preventionTips: Use fresh, properly stored hops and separate hot-break/hop trub before pitching.
Maintain clean cold-side sanitation and rack off yeast in a timely manner.
whenAppropriate: Always a fault.

name: Chlorophenol
description: Sharp medicinal, Band-Aid, antiseptic mouthwash, or burnt-plastic character from chlorinated water reacting with yeast.
aromaPerception: Band-Aid adhesive, hospital antiseptic, Chloraseptic throat spray, or electrical plastic.
flavorPerception: Harsh medicinal, plastic, or antiseptic flavor that lingers.
mouthfeelPerception: Slight chemical numbing or medicinal dryness.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Clean Phenolic (4-VG): Yeast phenols taste like natural clove, pepper, or smoke; chlorophenols smell unmistakably like Band-Aids, mouthwash, or hospital antiseptic.
vs. Metallic: Metallic tastes like pennies or blood on the tongue; chlorophenol smells and tastes like medicinal plastic.
typicalOrigins: Brewing with municipal tap water containing chlorine or chloramine.
Rinsing fermenters or bottles with bleach-based sanitizers without thorough rinsing.
Wild yeast contamination amplifying phenolic reactions.
preventionTips: Treat all brewing and sparge water with Campden tablets (potassium metabisulfite) or activated carbon filtration.
Never use chlorine bleach on brewing equipment—use no-rinse acid/peracetic sanitizers (Star San, Saniclean).
whenAppropriate: Always a severe fault.

name: Lightstruck (Skunky)
description: Unmistakable skunk-spray aroma caused by UV or blue light photolyzing hop iso-alpha acids.
aromaPerception: Fresh skunk spray, burnt rubber musk, or sun-struck green-bottle lager.
flavorPerception: Sharp, skunky, sulfurous hop bitterness.
mouthfeelPerception: No direct mouthfeel impact.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Catty: Catty smells like tomcat urine or blackcurrant leaves; lightstruck smells strictly like skunk spray.
vs. Dank Hops: Dank hops smell resinous, earthy, and herbal/cannabis-like; lightstruck is acrid, sulfurous skunk spray.
typicalOrigins: Exposure of hopped beer to sunlight (UV) or fluorescent store lighting.
Packaging in clear or green glass bottles without light-stable hop extracts.
preventionTips: Package beer in amber/brown glass bottles, aluminum cans, or stainless kegs.
Store bottles in closed boxes away from sunlight and fluorescent lights.
whenAppropriate: Always a fault (even in classic green-bottle import lagers, though judges occasionally note it as a packaging reality).

name: Metallic
description: Copper coin, blood-like, tin-can, or rusty-iron taste that coats the tongue.
aromaPerception: None or very faint tin/blood-like metallic edge.
flavorPerception: Sucking on a copper penny, blood, tin can, or fountain-pen ink.
mouthfeelPerception: Slight sharp, prickly, astringent metallic coating on the tongue.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Astringent: Astringency dries and puckers the gums like black tea; metallic tastes specifically like blood, tin, or a penny in your mouth.
vs. Minerally Water: High-sulfate/chloride water tastes crisp or chalky; iron/copper ions taste distinctively like coins or blood.
typicalOrigins: High iron or manganese in well/tap brewing water.
Unpassivated stainless steel, chipped enamel kettles, or acidic beer/wort contacting iron, brass, or mild steel.
Lipid oxidation in poorly stored pale malts.
preventionTips: Filter iron-rich brewing water and avoid brewing with chipped enamel or non-stainless fittings.
Passivate new stainless steel equipment with citric or nitric acid.
whenAppropriate: Always a fault.

name: Musty / Corked
description: Damp basement, wet soil, mildew, or moldy wine-cork character from TCA or mold contamination.
aromaPerception: Damp cellar, wet basement, mildew, moldy cork, or damp potting soil.
flavorPerception: Earthy, moldy, damp cellar flavor that strips away fresh fruit and hop notes.
mouthfeelPerception: Slightly flat or muted finish.
diagnosticContrasts: vs. Earthy Hops (Fuggle/Golding): Earthy hops smell like clean dry forest floor or tea leaves; musty/corked smells damp, moldy, and like a wet cellar.
vs. Oxidized / Cardboard: Cardboard is papery; musty is moldy, damp soil or cork taint.
typicalOrigins: Moldy grain, contaminated natural corks, or damp wooden barrels.
Chlorine sanitizer contacting mold/phenols in the brewery (forming TCA).
Geosmin in unfiltered municipal water during seasonal algae blooms.
preventionTips: Keep malt storage dry, inspect corks and barrels, and never use chlorine near damp wood or cellar spaces.
Carbon-filter brewing water if municipal water tastes earthy.
whenAppropriate: Always a fault.
